What to note: copy the exact wording as it appears (capitalisation, “Borough/City/County”), and copy the homepage URL.

2) Find the fee changes and decision papers
Search the council site for any of these pages — use the site search box or Google with: site:yourcouncil.gov.uk "event fees" OR "fees and charges" OR "events charges" OR "licensing fees".
Key places to check:
- “Fees and charges” or “Prices and payments” page (often under “Services” or “Business/Events”): will show the published old/new fee schedules.
- “Council meetings / agendas & minutes / committee reports”: look for the date when the fee increase was decided. Search for agendas/minutes for Cabinet, Communities, Leisure, Events, or Licensing committees around the decision date.
- “News / press releases” or “Consultations”: sometimes the council announces changes here with a summary and links to the report.
- “Parks, open spaces, events” or “Licensing & permits” service pages: those pages may list event fees or have a PDF of charges.
What to extract and record:
- Exact council name as used on site.
- Document/report title, date of meeting and decision, decision reference (if shown).
- The fee schedule: list the specific event types affected (e.g., “small community event — old £X, new £Y”), or a headline % increase.
- Implementation date / effective date for the new fees.
- Any cited impact assessment or consultation documents (EQIA, financial appendix).
How to use Google if the site search is weak:
- Google operator example: site:yourcouncil.gov.uk "fees and charges" "events"
- Or search by committee: site:yourcouncil.gov.uk "cabinet" "agenda" "event fees" and include the month/year.

3) If you can’t find decision papers
- Use the agendas & minutes section first — committee reports that recommend fee changes are usually uploaded with the agenda as a PDF.
- If still missing, file the FOI request (template I prepared earlier) asking for the committee report, impact assessments and communications.

How to calculate a reasonable estimated loss for the cancelled summer fete

1) Collect the fete’s usual income and costs (use last year’s figures or reasonable estimates)
Income items (typical):
- Pitch/stall fees (number of stalls × fee per stall)
- Ticket sales or entry donations
- Food/drink sales revenue (if the organising group runs stalls)
- Raffle/sponsorship/donations
- Bar or refreshment takings
Costs you would have incurred (typical):
- Site hire / council event fee (the one that has risen)
- Insurance
- Stage/equipment hire (PA, generators)
- Utilities and portaloos
- Entertainment/performers (fees)
- Security/first aid
- Marketing/print materials
- Volunteer expenses / staff costs (if any)
- Licences and temporary event notices

2) Basic formula
Net loss (what you want to report) = Estimated lost income − Costs saved by not running the event.
Notes:
- Some costs are sunk (non-refundable deposits) — include them if you had already paid.
- “Costs saved” are what you would not have had to pay because the event didn’t happen (e.g., if you cancel before paying for stage hire you save that cost).
- If the council fee was the main reason for cancelling, it’s valid to highlight the direct extra cost that triggered the decision and the knock-on lost income.

3) Quick worked example (adjust numbers to your situation)
Assume:
- 30 stall pitches × £20 = £600
- Ticket/donations = £400
- Raffle/sponsorship = £200
Total potential income = £1,200

Costs that would have been paid:
- Council event fee (new) = £600 (old was £200 — a £400 extra)
- Stage & PA hire = £300
- Insurance = £120
- Portaloos = £80
- Marketing = £100
Total costs = £1,200

If the group cancels, you avoid some costs (stage hire refundable? assume not refunded), but you lose all the income. Net effect:
- If costs are non-refundable £1,000 and you lose £1,200 income → net loss = £1,200 (lost income) − £200 (costs avoided) = £1,000
- Or, emphasise the immediate direct loss caused by the fee change: we would have faced an extra £400 in fees, making the event unviable, and an overall projected shortfall of ~£1,000 which forced cancellation.

4) If you need a conservative public figure to put in petitions/emails
- Use verifiable or easily defended numbers: e.g., “Projected loss: approximately £1,000 — based on usual stall fees (£X), ticket income (£Y) and commitments for hired equipment (£Z).”
- If uncertain, give a range: “Estimated loss: £800–£1,200” and say how you calculated it briefly in a line.

- Request fee waiver if the disclosure is in the public interest; explain how it will contribute to public understanding and that you have no commercial interest.

- Site plan: Pick a clear start/finish point, staging area, restroom access, water, shade, and an accessible route for people with mobility needs.  
- Roles & contacts: Assign lead organizer, safety marshals/volunteers, first‑aid person, media contact, legal observer (if desired), logistics lead, and clean‑up crew. Share a phone tree or group chat for coordinators.  
- Supplies: First‑aid kit, water, sunscreen, trash bags, portable chargers, printed agenda/handouts, signage/sticks, high‑visibility vests for marshals, trash/recycling bins.  
- Accessibility & inclusion: Provide a quiet area, seating if possible, ASL interpreters or captioning info if available, and clear directions for how to participate for those who cannot stand long.  
- Communication plan: Designate a single media contact and a separate person for participant questions. Have a plan to share updates (social post, text chain).  
- Safety & de‑escalation: Brief marshals on how to handle confrontations calmly, and when to call law enforcement. Train marshals on safe distancing, keeping crowd flow, and protecting vulnerable attendees.  
- Photography & privacy: Post or state that photos may be taken; explain how images will be used. Respect requests not to be photographed.  
- Contingency planning: Prepare for weather, counter‑demonstrations, or sudden site changes. Have an agreed evacuation route and rendezvous point.  
- Liability & insurance: If available, check event insurance or rely on venue/permit requirements; know whether organizers assume any liability.  
- Clean‑up: Plan to leave the site as you found it; assign a crew to collect trash immediately after.

- Respect & conduct: “Please be respectful; do not block sidewalks or private property. If you see a safety concern, alert a marshal.”  
- Media & photos: “Our media contact is [name]. By attending you may be photographed; if you prefer not to be, tell a marshal.”  
- Closing & cleanup: “Please stay for a 10‑minute cleanup after we finish. If you’d like to help organize future information sessions, sign up at [table/link].”
